q: The base of the Great Pyramid at Giza covers roughly how much area compared to St. Peter's Basilica in Rome?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The Great Pyramid's base, 230.25 meters per side, covers roughly twice the area of St. Peter's Basilica in Rome.

q: Which pharaoh built the original Temple of Khonsu at Karnak?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: Rameses III built the original Temple of Khonsu; Taharqo later modified it, and later rulers added its gateway and hypostyle hall.

q: What two ornamental motifs decorate the Erechtheion?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: The Erechtheion uses both egg & tongue and egg & dart ornament.

q: What gives the Red Pyramid of Sneferu, also called the Shining Northern Pyramid, its name?
o: Red paint applied to its casing
Its location beside a red-sand desert
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The Red Pyramid takes its name from the reddish limestone used to build most of its core, and stands about 104 meters high.

q: Where within the fortress of Mycenae is the Lion Gate positioned?
o: At the summit of the acropolis
The northwest wall of the fortress
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Aegean
n: The Lion Gate serves as the main entrance to the citadel, located in the northwest wall of the fortress at Mycenae.

q: What is the Theater of Dionysus considered the architectural prototype for?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: The Theater of Dionysus in Athens is considered the prototype for all Greek theaters.

q: Who were the two architects of the Parthenon?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: The Parthenon, dedicated to Athena and the largest Greek temple, was designed by Ictinus and Kallikrates.

q: At roughly what angle does the lower portion of the Bent Pyramid of Sneferu rise?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The Bent Pyramid begins at about 54 degrees before shifting to a shallower 42 degrees halfway up.

q: A temple front with ten columns is described using which term?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Two Ways of Describing Temples
n: Ten columns across the front is termed decastyle.

q: An "octastyle" temple front has how many columns?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Two Ways of Describing Temples
n: The prefix "octa-" refers to eight, so an octastyle front carries eight columns.

q: A temple front with six columns is described using which term?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Two Ways of Describing Temples
n: Six columns across the entrance front is termed hexastyle.

q: Who is credited as the architect of the Step Pyramid of Djoser (Zoser) at Saqqara?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: Imhotep designed the Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara, considered the oldest surviving masonry building structure.

q: Which term describes the tightest possible spacing between columns?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Intercolumnation
n: Pycnostyle ("tight-columned") has the smallest ratio, about 1.50, the closest spacing of the five classical intercolumniation types.

q: Who designed the Theater of Epidaurus, noted as the most beautiful and best-preserved Greek theater?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: Polykleitus the Younger designed the Theater of Epidaurus, regarded as the most beautiful and preserved Greek theater.

q: What makes the Step Pyramid of Djoser especially significant in architectural history?
o: It is the tallest pyramid in Egypt
It was the first pyramid faced in reddish limestone
It is the oldest surviving masonry building structure
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara is regarded as the oldest surviving masonry building structure in history.

q: What two timekeeping functions did the Tower of the Winds in Athens combine?
o: Two separate sundials, one for each solstice
A sundial inside and a water-clock outside
A water-clock inside and a sundial outside
A bell tower and a solar calendar
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: The octagonal Tower of the Winds functioned as a water-clock (clepsydra) internally and a sundial externally.

q: A temple front with nine columns is described using which term?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Two Ways of Describing Temples
n: Nine columns across the front is termed enneastyle.

q: Roughly how many times its base width is the typical height of an Egyptian obelisk?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: Obelisks are tall, monumental, tapering stone shafts whose height usually runs about 9 to 10 times the size of the base.

q: "Systyle," or "close-columned" spacing, corresponds to roughly what ratio?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Intercolumnation
n: Systyle sits between pycnostyle (1.50) and eustyle (2.25), at about 2.00.

q: Which term describes a temple with columns across both the front and the rear, but not along the sides?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Arrangement of Greek Temples
n: Amphiprostyle adds a second row of columns at the back to the front-only prostyle arrangement, without side colonnades.

q: How many colossal seated statues stand at the entrance facade of Abu Simbel, and roughly how tall are they?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: Abu Simbel's imposing rock-cut facade fronts four colossal seated statues, each over 20 meters (about 65 feet) high.

q: Who designed the Propylaea of Athens, and under whose leadership was it built?
o: Designed by Ictinus, built under Cimon
Designed by Kallikrates, built under Solon
Designed by Phidias, built under Themistocles
Designed by Mnesicles, built under Pericles
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: The Propylaea, the imposing entrance to the Acropolis, was designed by Mnesicles and built under Pericles.

q: "Eustyle," meaning "well-columned," corresponds to roughly what spacing ratio?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Intercolumnation
n: Eustyle sits in the middle of the five terms, considered the most visually balanced spacing at about 2.25.

q: An Egyptian sphinx combining a lion's body with a human head is called what?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The androsphinx combines a lion's body with a man's head; the ram-headed and hawk-headed forms are named separately.

q: Which three classical orders appear together in the design of the Temple of Apollo Epicurius?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: The Temple of Apollo Epicurius at Bassae is unusual for combining Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian elements in a single peripteral, hexastyle design.

q: Which principle of Greek architecture concerns the balanced relationship among a structure's parts?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures
n: Perfection of proportions refers to the balanced, harmonious sizing of a building's architectural elements relative to one another.

q: Roughly how tall is the Meidum Pyramid of Sneferu?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The Meidum Pyramid of Sneferu stands about 92 meters high and was the first ground pyramid built with an above-ground burial chamber.

q: What architectural form is the Treasury of Atreus (Tomb of Agamemnon)?
o: A megaron with a central hearth
A tholos, or beehive-corbelled domed stone vault
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Aegean
n: The Treasury of Atreus is a tholos tomb, a beehive-corbelled domed stone vault, located on Panagitsa Hill at Mycenae.

q: A Greek temple plan surrounded by two complete rows of columns is classified as what?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Arrangement of Greek Temples
n: A dipteral temple is enclosed by a double row of surrounding columns, unlike the single row of a peripteral plan.

q: A temple front with five columns is described using which term?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Two Ways of Describing Temples
n: Five columns across the front is termed pentastyle.

q: Why is the Temple of Amon at Karnak considered architecturally unique among Egyptian temples?
o: It was not built to one complete plan, but grew through contributions of many kings over centuries
It is the only rock-cut temple in Egypt
It was built entirely by a single pharaoh in one reign
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: Unlike temples built to a single design, the Temple of Amon at Karnak owes its size, disposition, and magnificence to the work of many kings, from the XIIth Dynasty through the Ptolemaic period.

q: Which distinctive carved figures are associated with the Temple of Zeus Olympus at Agrigentum?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: The Temple of Zeus Olympus is noted for its Atlantes, large carved male figures, and for having 104 columns.

q: Which broad term refers to any mosaic made of regularly cut material?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Roman Concrete Walls
n: Opus Sectile is the general term for mosaics of regularly cut pieces; opus alexandrinum and opus vermiculatum are its specific variants.

q: A temple front with a single column is described using which term?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Two Ways of Describing Temples
n: A single-column front is termed henostyle, the smallest classification in this naming system.

q: Which Roman walling technique produced a net-like diagonal pattern using small pyramidal stones?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Roman Concrete Walls
n: Opus Reticulatum used small pyramidal stones with square exposed bases set diagonally in a concrete core, their fine joints forming a net-like mesh pattern.

q: Who designed the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, reportedly under the patronage of Alexander the Great?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: Deinocrates designed the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus during the time of Alexander the Great; Scopas served as sculptor.

q: A temple front with four columns is described using which term?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Two Ways of Describing Temples
n: Greek temple fronts are named for their column count using Greek numerical prefixes; four columns is tetrastyle.

q: Which pharaoh began construction of the Temple of Luxor?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: Amenhotep III began the Temple of Luxor, which was completed by Tutankhamun and Horemheb and later added to by Rameses II.

q: Greek architecture is characterized by simplicity and harmony, purity of lines, perfection of proportions, and which fourth quality?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures
n: The four defining qualities of Greek architecture are simplicity & harmony, purity of lines, perfection of proportions, and refinement of details.

q: Who led the major excavation of the whole site of Knossos, beginning around 1900?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Aegean
n: Sir Arthur Evans excavated the whole of Knossos from around March 1900 to 1931, following Kalokairinos's initial 1878 dig.

q: What architectural first is credited to the Meidum Pyramid of Sneferu?
o: The first pyramid with a bent profile
The first pyramid built at Giza
The first ground pyramid with an above-ground burial chamber
The first pyramid faced in limestone casing
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The Meidum Pyramid was the first ground pyramid to have its burial chamber built above ground; it originally rose as a 7-step pyramid.

q: Who commissioned the Great Pyramid at Giza?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The Great Pyramid at Giza, also called the Pyramid of Khufu or Cheops, was built for Khufu.

q: To what is the Temple of Nike Apteros, on the Athenian Acropolis, dedicated?
o: Athena as protector of the city
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: Designed by Kallikrates in an Ionic, amphi-prostyle, tetrastyle plan, the Temple of Nike Apteros is dedicated to the "wingless victory."

q: Which variant of opus sectile used geometric patterns in a limited palette, such as black and white or dark green and red?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Roman Concrete Walls
n: Opus Alexandrinum is a form of opus sectile restricted to a few colors arranged in geometric patterns.

q: The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus served as the ceremonial center for which festival?
o: The Pan-Ionic festival of the Asiatic colonies
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: As a Hellenistic, Ionic, dipteral, octastyle temple, the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus was the center of the Pan-Ionic festival of the Asiatic colonies.

q: What is the present height of the Pyramid of Khafra (Chephren) at Giza?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The Pyramid of Khafra originally rose 143.50 meters; its present height is about 136.40 meters.

q: What classical order and plan type is the Parthenon?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: The Parthenon is Doric in order, peripteral in plan (a single surrounding colonnade), and octastyle (eight columns across the front).

q: After centuries buried beneath streets and houses, what was later built over the uncovered Temple of Luxor?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The Temple of Luxor was eventually built over by the mosque of Sufi Shaykh Yusuf Abu al-Hajjaj, which was carefully preserved as the temple was uncovered.

q: What is the base length of the Pyramid of Menkaure (Mykerinos) at Giza?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The Pyramid of Menkaure, the smallest of the three great Giza pyramids, has a base of about 103.40 meters.

q: Who first excavated the Palace of Minos at Knossos, in 1878?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Aegean
n: Minos Kalokairinos carried out the first excavation of Knossos in 1878, decades before Sir Arthur Evans's major excavation.

q: What are the massive sloping gateway towers fronting many Egyptian temples called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: Pylons are massive sloping towers that front Egyptian temples, typically flanked by obelisks, functioning as monumental gateways.

q: Which term describes a temple with columns placed only across its front?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Arrangement of Greek Temples
n: Prostyle temples carry columns only on the entrance front, unlike amphiprostyle temples which add a matching row at the rear.

q: In which city is the Temple of Apollo Epicurius located?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: The Temple of Apollo Epicurius, designed by Iktinos and dedicated to Apollo Epikourios, is located at Bassae.

q: The Mastaba of Thi at Sakkara was built for a man who also held which position?
o: Royal Architect and manager of pyramids
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: Thi, whose well-preserved and restored mastaba stands at Sakkara, held the position of Royal Architect and manager of pyramids.

q: In which city was the Temple of Zeus Olympus (460 BC) built?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: The Temple of Zeus Olympus was built at Agrigentum, designed by Libon of Elis and later rebuilt with the involvement of the Roman architect Cossutius.

q: An Egyptian sphinx with the head of a ram is called what?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The criosphinx pairs a lion's body with a ram's head.

q: An Egyptian sphinx with the head of a hawk is called what?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The hieracosphinx pairs a lion's body with a hawk's head.

q: Which Roman technique used specially made triangular bricks (in plan) for facing walls?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Roman Concrete Walls
n: Opus Testaceum faced walls with bricks made triangular in plan.

q: In which region is the Great Temple of Abu Simbel located?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The Great Temple of Abu Simbel is a rock-hewn temple located in Nubia.

q: In what years was the Parthenon built?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: The Parthenon was constructed from 447 to 432 BC.

q: Which term describes a circular Greek temple form?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Arrangement of Greek Temples
n: Tholos designates a circular temple plan, distinct from the rectangular anta, prostyle, and peripteral forms.

q: What does "Mammisi," the name given to a distinct Egyptian temple type, mean?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: Mammisi means "Birth House," and this temple type became the prototype for the Greek Doric temple.

q: Who sculpted the decorative program of the Parthenon?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: Phidias served as master sculptor for the Parthenon.

q: Which mosaic technique arranged tessera in wavy lines resembling worm tracks?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Roman Concrete Walls
n: Opus Vermiculatum takes its name from the Latin for "worm," describing its wavy, worm-track-like tessera pattern.

q: Which pharaoh built the Mammisi Temple?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: Nectanebo II built the Mammisi Temple, whose form went on to prototype the Greek Doric temple.

q: How does the Treasury of Atreus compare to Mycenae's other tholos tombs?
o: It is the smallest of the tombs
It predates all the other tholos tombs by centuries
It is the only tholos tomb without a dromos
It is the largest and best preserved of the nine tholos tombs
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Aegean
n: The Treasury of Atreus is described as the largest and best-preserved of the nine tholos tombs at Mycenae.

q: The Bent Pyramid of Sneferu is notable as the first pyramid to use what?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The Bent Pyramid was the first pyramid to use limestone casing, standing about 105 meters high.

q: A temple front with only two columns is described using which term?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Two Ways of Describing Temples
n: Two columns across the front is termed distyle.

q: What plan type describes the Erechtheion?
o: Ionic, apteral, irregular plan with no side colonnades
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: Unlike more regular temple plans, the Erechtheion is Ionic and apteral, with an irregular plan and no side colonnades — accommodating its caryatid and other porches.

q: Who built the Olympion in Athens?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: The Olympion, a Corinthian, dipteral, octastyle structure designed with Cossutius's involvement, was built by Antiochus Epiphanes.

q: Which Roman walling technique used small, rough stones laid loosely, roughly resembling polygonal masonry?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Roman Concrete Walls
n: Opus Incertum used small stones set irregularly in mortar, sometimes interrupted by courses of brick or tile.

q: Roughly how many spectators could the Theater of Dionysus in Athens accommodate?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: The Theater of Dionysus, site of the Panathenaic festivals and choragic competitions, could accommodate almost 18,000 spectators and is considered the prototype of all Greek theaters.

q: A temple front with three columns is described using which term?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Two Ways of Describing Temples
n: Three columns across the front is termed tristyle.

q: Which term describes a dipteral-style temple where the inner row of columns has been omitted, widening the space around the naos?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Arrangement of Greek Temples
n: Pseudodipteral temples drop the inner colonnade of a true dipteral plan, leaving a wider gap between the naos and the remaining outer row.

q: Why does the Bent Pyramid of Sneferu change its angle of slope partway up?
o: To align with the rising sun
To lighten the structure and prevent it from collapsing
To match the height of a nearby pyramid
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The Bent Pyramid's lower portion rises at 54 degrees before shifting to 42 degrees halfway up, a change made to lighten the pyramid and prevent it from collapsing.

q: In Greek temple plans, what is the small chamber sometimes found at the rear of the naos called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Arrangement of Greek Temples
n: The opisthodomos is a rear chamber behind the naos, appearing in plans such as the double anta and peripteral types.

q: Which classical intercolumniation term describes the widest, most open spacing between columns?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Intercolumnation
n: Araeostyle ("light-columned") is the widest spacing of the five terms, with a ratio of about 4.00.

q: By tradition, roughly how long did it take to build an Egyptian pyramid, and with how much labor?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The traditional account holds that pyramids were built by roughly 100 men over about 100 years, oriented with their four sides facing the cardinal points.

q: How does the Temple of Zeus Olympus rank in scale among Doric Greek temples?
o: It is the smallest known Doric temple
It is the largest Doric Greek temple
It ranks third in size after the Parthenon and the Olympion
It is the second largest Doric Greek temple
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: The Temple of Zeus Olympus at Agrigentum is described as the second largest Doric Greek temple, after the Parthenon.

q: What was the Choragic Monument of Lysicrates built to display and commemorate?
o: A statue of the choregos himself
A tripod, awarded as a prize in athletic or musical competitions
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: The Corinthian-order Choragic Monument of Lysicrates was erected to support a tripod, a type of prize awarded for victory in athletic or musical competitions at Greek festivals.

q: Which of these is NOT one of the Roman concrete/masonry wall techniques described?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Roman Concrete Walls
n: Opus Pulvinatum is not among the named techniques; the recognized types include Quadratum, Incertum, Reticulatum, Testaceum, Mixtum, Sectile, Alexandrinum, and Vermiculatum.

q: During the Christian era, what did the hypostyle hall of the Temple of Luxor become?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The hypostyle hall of the Temple of Luxor was converted into a Christian church during the Christian era, and remains of a Coptic church can still be seen nearby.

q: By what other name is the Tower of the Winds in Athens known?
o: The Horologion of Andronikos Kyrrhestes, or Clepsydra
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: The octagonal Tower of the Winds is also known as the Horologion of Andronikos Kyrrhestes, or Clepsydra.

q: What is the innermost chamber of a Greek temple, housing the cult statue, called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Arrangement of Greek Temples
n: The naos, also called the cella, is the enclosed inner chamber that held the temple's cult image.

q: Which term names a "broad-columned" spacing, with a ratio of about 3.00?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Intercolumnation
n: Diastyle describes a wider, more open spacing than eustyle, at roughly 3.00.

q: A temple front with eight columns is described using which term?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Two Ways of Describing Temples
n: Eight columns across the entrance front is termed octastyle.

q: What holds the dome of the Treasury of Atreus together, in place of columns or other support?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Aegean
n: The Treasury of Atreus was the first structure built without columns or other support, its dome held together by a single keystone.

q: Which technique alternated bands of "tufa" within ordinary brick facing, or mixed rectangular and small squared stone blocks?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Roman Concrete Walls
n: Opus Mixtum combined different wall-surface materials, introducing tufa bands into brick facing or alternating stone block sizes.

q: A spacing ratio of about 4.00 corresponds to which intercolumniation term?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Intercolumnation
n: A ratio near 4.00 is the widest of the five terms, called araeostyle.

q: A Greek temple plan surrounded by a single, unbroken row of freestanding columns is classified as what?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Arrangement of Greek Temples
n: A peripteral temple has a single colonnade of freestanding columns running completely around the naos.

q: Who was the architect of the Temple of Queen Hatshepsut at Deir-el-Bahri?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: Senenmut designed the Temple of Queen Hatshepsut, on the west bank of the Nile at Mt. Deir-el-Bahri.

q: In which modern city and island is the Palace of Minos located?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Aegean
n: The Palace of Minos, a Minoan palace, is located at Heraklion on the island of Crete.

q: What is the present height of the Great Pyramid at Giza, after losing its outer casing?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The Great Pyramid originally stood 146.64 meters tall; its present height, without its lost outer casing, is about 137.20 meters.

q: On which bank of the Nile, and at what site, does the Temple of Queen Hatshepsut stand?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The Temple of Queen Hatshepsut sits on the West Bank of the Nile at Mt. Deir-el-Bahri.

q: A spacing ratio of about 2.25 corresponds to which intercolumniation term?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Intercolumnation
n: A ratio of roughly 2.25 defines eustyle, the "well-columned" spacing regarded as most harmonious.

q: Besides mortar, what additional fasteners could secure the stone blocks of Opus Quadratum?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Roman Concrete Walls
n: Opus Quadratum blocks were frequently secured with dowels and cramps in addition to, or instead of, mortar joints.

q: What is the porch or vestibule leading into the naos of a Greek temple called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Arrangement of Greek Temples
n: The pronaos is the entrance porch in front of the naos, seen in the simple anta-type temple plan.

q: A spacing ratio of about 1.50 corresponds to which intercolumniation term?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Intercolumnation
n: A ratio near 1.50 is the tightest of the five terms, called pycnostyle.

q: Rock-cut (rock-hewn) tombs, carved directly from native rock with only a front facade and dark interior chambers, were built for whom?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: Rock-cut tombs were tombs of nobility, hewn from the rock so that only an architectural front was visible, leading to dark interior chambers.

q: Which term describes a temple that appears peripteral, but whose surrounding columns are actually engaged to the cella wall rather than freestanding?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Arrangement of Greek Temples
n: Pseudoperipteral temples attach (engage) the outer columns to the wall, giving the visual effect of a peripteral colonnade without true freestanding columns.

q: Which Egyptian tomb structure has a flat or tapered top and served as a solid burial form?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The mastaba is a flat-topped or tapered solid tomb structure, an early form that preceded the true pyramid.

q: A temple front with seven columns is described using which term?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Two Ways of Describing Temples
n: Seven columns across the front is termed heptastyle.

q: A temple front with twelve columns is described using which term?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Two Ways of Describing Temples
n: Twelve columns across the front is termed dodecastyle, the largest classification listed.

q: What construction technique is associated with the Lion Gate at Mycenae?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Aegean
n: The Lion Gate is built of conglomerate ashlar and forms the main entrance to the citadel of Mycenae.

q: Which Roman walling technique consisted of squared stone blocks laid in regular ashlar courses?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 35 — Roman Concrete Walls
n: Opus Quadratum used rectangular blocks of stone, sometimes with dowels and cramps rather than mortar, laid in regular ashlar courses.

q: What distinguishes a mortuary temple from a cult temple in Egyptian architecture?
o: A mortuary temple honors a deceased, deified king; a cult temple worships a god
A cult temple is only built underground
There is no real difference between them
A mortuary temple is smaller in scale
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: Mortuary temples were built in honor of pharaohs for offerings and worship of the deceased, deified king, while cult temples were devoted to the worship of a divinity.

q: In which city is the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, located?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: The Temple of Artemis, designed by Deinocrates and counted among the Seven Wonders of the World, stood at Ephesus.

q: To which deity, and at which site, were obelisks originally erected as a cult symbol?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: Obelisks were originally erected as a cult symbol of the sun god at Heliopolis, and were typically covered with hieroglyphs.

q: How many columns border the peristyle court of the Temple of Khonsu at Karnak?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 36 — Egyptian Structures
n: The Temple of Khonsu's peristyle court is bordered by 28 columns, and is considered an almost complete New Kingdom temple.

q: Which Athenian structure is especially known for its caryatid porch?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 37 — Greek Structures: Hellenic
n: The Erechtheion, built 421 to 406 BC, uses a caryatid porch, often called the South Porch.
